column1: # Every capstone decode in scripts/ whose byte range is measured FROM THE DECODE START.
# `scripts/check-decode-extent-bounds.py` finds them by AST and requires each one to appear here.
# The gate goes RED on a site with no row AND on a row matching no site, so this file is an
# inventory rather than a mute button: it cannot go quiet by drifting out of date.
# WHY EVERY ROW HERE IS A CLAIM WORTH CHECKING. A byte budget from a function entry is the shape
# of all five instances of the decode-past-the-end class (see the gate's docstring). The fifth,
# found on 2026-08-31, had been TUNED: `check-singleton-field-offsets.py` picked its window size
# to keep a `CS::GameMan +0x0` "vftable slot" that turns out to decode as
# `sar dword ptr [rax], 0x6f` in bytes past a `ret`. So "it has been like that for a while and
# the numbers look right" is not a reason. The reason has to say what actually stops the decode.
# columns: path <TAB> function <TAB> span <TAB> status <TAB> reason
#   cap-on-extent      the real stop is an extent or a terminator rule; the count only bounds a
#                      runaway, and reaching it is reported rather than papered over
#   extent-elsewhere   the span IS an extent, just carried in from another source (Ghidra, .pdata)
#   single-instruction the decode consumes one instruction; 15 bytes is the x86-64 maximum
#   operator-supplied  the window is named by the person running the tool, per invocation
#   dumper             prints for a human and decides no verdict
#   kept-fixture       a deliberately WRONG decode, preserved and asserted against
#   foreign-binary     ersc.dll, an ordinary MSVC DLL with real .pdata and real int3 padding --
#                      not one of the de-Arxan'd ELDEN RING images this class lives in
#   OPEN               a genuine byte budget that can leave the function. NOT fixed. The gate
#                      prints these every run with their reason.
# --- objdump spans (matched by text, not by AST: the range is built for a subprocess) ---------

column5: `size` is the body length Ghidra declares for the function, read out of the functions TSV -- an extent from a second authority rather than a budget. The function also returns None when `consumed < size - 15`, so a decode that fell apart is reported as no-evidence instead of as a body.
Instance 1 itself, preserved as the discriminator for BRANCH_SCAN_CASES. Reverting `patch_safe` to this shape must make the selftest fail; that is the point of keeping it.

The pre-2026-08-30 trampoline walk, kept ON PURPOSE. `selftest` asserts that every refusal in PATCH_SAFE_CASES is one this thing gets WRONG, which is how "the bound matters" is measured every run instead of asserted in a comment. Fixing it would delete the mutation test.

`length = min(end - start, SIGNATURE_BYTES)` and `end` is the `.pdata` extent of the function being signed, so the extent wins whenever it is the smaller of the two. The input set is `.pdata`-declared functions only.

`stop = va + count * 16` is slack for `--count` instructions, and the comparison is truncated to `min(len(dump), len(deobf))`. The Ghidra side is asked for `length: count * 8` over the same VA, so BOTH sides read past the function end together and a shared over-read cannot manufacture the disagreement this tool reports.

The loop breaks on `insn.address + insn.size > function_extent.body_end(...)`, added 2026-08-31 as the fix for instance 5; 64 is slack for FOLLOW_INSNS instructions and is reached only when the extent is unknown (2 sites, measured). The bound is inside the loop rather than on the slice because the walk also stops on a register clobber and on a branch.

`length` is `drift.KNOWN["length"]` -- the hand-derived 24-byte body of `GetScadutreeBlessing`, this tool's pinned positive control. The production paths in the same file take `drift.extent_of(...)`, which is the shared rule.
The 1.17 half of the same pinned control pair.
`--bytes N`, typed by the operator, printed to a terminal; the loop additionally breaks at the first `ret`. It decides nothing.
`disas-deobf.sh <VA> [nbytes]`: the operator types the length and reads the output in a terminal. It decides nothing and writes nothing.
Same shape, Intel syntax, default 256 bytes, printed for a human.
`objdump -s` -- a HEX DUMP of `.rdata`/`.data`, not a disassembly at all. There is no instruction stream to fall out of phase.

Three terminator rules stop this walk before the slice can: the first `jmp` (the tail jump it is looking for), the first `ret`, and `insn.address - va > MAX_TRAMPOLINE_INSNS * 8` = 192 bytes. 256 is slack above that last bound so a long instruction cannot be truncated mid-decode. Reaching the end is REPORTED rather than guessed at: the function returns kind `undecoded`, and every caller keeps the kind, so a trampoline that did not resolve is visible in the output instead of being reported as a handler address.

`nbytes` is the `-n` the operator passes on the command line, defaulting to 0x120, and the listing stops at the first `ret` unless `--no-stop` is given -- reading PAST the end is the point of that flag (it is how the v2.0.0 option actions' relocated return blocks were found). The output is a human-facing dump that decides no verdict; every address this tool produced was then confirmed by `.pdata` index, function size, or an xref, never by the listing alone. ersc.dll is not de-Arxan'd either: real .pdata, real int3 padding.

A `n`-byte hexdump-with-mnemonics of ersc.dll for a human, and it PRINTS where the decode stopped short. ersc.dll is not de-Arxan'd: it has real `.pdata` and real int3 padding, so the resynchronisation this class is about does not arise.

The span is a whole `.text` SECTION (raw pointer to raw/virtual size), not a function -- a deliberate linear sweep of ersc.dll to build an xref index, with `skipdata` on so an undecodable byte does not desynchronise the rest.

A `Game.Debug.*` getter stub is a `jmp rel32` or a `movzx`/`ret` pair, and the decode is `count=STUB_MAX_INSNS`-limited on top of the 32-byte slice, so the walk stops on instruction count long before the slice does. It reads only the first operand it finds and returns None otherwise; a resynchronised byte past the stub cannot become an answer because there is no answer to give past instruction STUB_MAX_INSNS.

`start` comes from the `--caller` VA the operator names on the command line, and every hit is PRINTED for a human to adjudicate rather than fed to a gate. Nothing downstream consumes this output as a measurement, so an over-read shows up as an obviously wrong line on a terminal, not as a silent fact in a ledger.

`count=1`: this decodes exactly ONE instruction at each candidate start while walking backwards from a displacement hit, and MAX_INSN_LEN is the x86-64 maximum so the slice can never hold two. The result is discarded unless `insn.size > back`, i.e. unless the single instruction actually covers the displacement it was decoded to explain.
`objdump_first_instruction` takes the first line of output for one address and discards the rest; the window exists only to give objdump something to decode.

A signature BUILDER over ersc.dll, not a body reader: it stops as soon as `want` bytes have been consumed, so `want * 3` is headroom for the instruction that straddles the limit. Overshooting a short function is expected and handled -- SIGNATURE_LADDER retries at 64, 48, 40, 32 and 24 bytes precisely because a long window reaches past a small function -- and the failure mode is a signature that matches nothing, never a wrong address. ersc.dll has real .pdata and real int3 padding, so the resynchronisation this class is about does not arise.

Two arms, two different stops, and only one of them ever needed the width. The `at_offset` arm consumes an instruction that STARTS exactly at a known byte offset, so no window size can invent one -- that is why `limit` opens to reach a reference at +0x779. The `n == index` fallback had no such protection and WAS a real over-read (fixed 2026-08-31): it is now gated on `function_extent.body_slice_end`, and refuses rather than answering when the extent is unknown. `limit` bounds a runaway only.

`* 3` is slack so that whole instructions can cover `want_bytes`; the loop stops at `consumed >= want_bytes` and, in the default `stop_at_return` mode used by `map_one`, at the first `ret`/`jmp` -- which is what keeps a short function's signature out of its neighbour. The `stop_at_return=False` mode is for a prologue GATE, where the byte count is the specification the runtime check will compare, not an inference about where the function ends.
Both lengths come from the CLI's `0x<addr>:<length>` pair spec, for a function the operator has already bounded. The pinned `SELFTEST_PAIR` carries a measured 24.

`re117_read.py <image> <va> <nbytes>` -- the operator types the length and reads the disassembly in a terminal. It writes nothing, decides no verdict, and has no caller; the point of the tool is to look at a range the operator has already chosen, including deliberately looking PAST a function end to see what is there.

`size` is the body length Ghidra declares, returned by `getFunctionByAddress` through `func_at` -- an extent from the dump rather than a budget this file chose. When the daemon omits it the default is 0, so the slice is EMPTY and `calls_in` returns no calls: the caller then finds no rel32 correspondence and the pair goes unresolved, which is a refusal rather than a decode over unknown bytes.
Returns on the FIRST decoded instruction. 20 is slack over the 15-byte x86-64 maximum, so the extra bytes are never decoded into a second instruction.
A grep over an operator-bounded disassembly window, printed for a human.

Slack for `--count` instructions, and the comparison is truncated to `min(len(dump), len(deobf))`. Both sides read the SAME byte range -- the Ghidra request is `length: count * 8` too -- so a shared over-read cannot manufacture a disagreement between them, which is the only thing this tool reports.

`window` is the declared `.pdata` extent whenever both images declare one, and `DECODE_BYTES` only when neither does. Hitting the count leaves the reason at STOP_LIMIT, and `compare` refuses to call a prefix identical -- so the cap costs a verdict rather than inventing one.
This IS the extent resolver -- the watermark sweep the whole repo defers to. It returns None when it reaches `limit` without a terminator, so the cap produces a refusal rather than a fabricated end.

The real bound is REACHABILITY: the first `ret`, or the first unconditional `jmp` that nothing decoded so far branches past. `MAX_BYTES` only stops a runaway, and reaching it returns `(None, None)`, which the caller reports as the NO-END verdict.
